article.headline: CodeMiko's Mocap Test Nails Real-Time Hand Contact Detection
article.lede: Virtual streamer CodeMiko has demonstrated a motion-capture test in which her 3D avatar faithfully reproduces hand-to-hand and hand-to-body contact — cracking knuckles, clapping, and slapping her belly — with correct collision response. The clip was captured live during a stream, with chat prompting the knuckle-crack in real time. It illustrates how far consumer-grade performance capture has moved toward solving one of the discipline's harder sub-problems.
article.body:
CodeMiko performs live as a high-fidelity 3D animated character, using real-time *motion capture* — a technique that translates a performer's physical movements into digital animation without post-production delay. Virtual streaming built on this technology has grown into a distinct genre, but most practitioners rely on face and body tracking alone, leaving hands either static or animated separately. Convincing hand interaction has remained stubbornly difficult.

The technical obstacle is *contact and collision detection*: two tracked objects (hands, or a hand and a torso) must register as touching rather than clipping through each other. In post-production film work, this is handled in compositing long after the fact. In a live stream, where there is no post-production window, the solver must infer contact geometry in milliseconds. Getting this wrong produces the uncanny image of hands phasing through one another, which breaks the illusion immediately.

Platforms tackling this problem — such as Reallusion's **Motion LIVE**, which unifies facial, body, and hand tracking through a single interface — have invested in precise *gesture capture* covering forearm, wrist, and individual finger movements. According to Reallusion's documentation, the system supports a range of mocap gloves and records detailed joint data in real time, enabling preview and editing of hand performances separately from body tracks. The challenge CodeMiko's clip addresses goes a step further: not just capturing the hands accurately, but resolving what happens when they meet.

The stream context matters. The chat prompt — 'Can you crack your knuckles?' — and the live audience counting subs in the corner underline that this is a real-time performance, not a pre-rendered showcase. That a viewer's one-line request could be executed on the spot, with visible contact fidelity, is the practical payoff of the test. For virtual performers who interact with audiences live, removing the visual glitch of clipping hands is a meaningful step toward presence.

concepts.definition: A technique that converts a performer's physical movements — tracked by cameras, sensors, or AI — into 3D character animation with no meaningful delay. Unlike studio mocap used in film, real-time systems must solve and render the animation within a single frame budget, making them harder to implement but essential for live performance.

The computational process of determining when two virtual objects occupy the same space and responding appropriately — preventing one from passing through the other. In real-time mocap, applying this to hands (which move fast and overlap in natural gestures) is especially demanding because the solver must act within milliseconds.

A live-stream performer who appears on screen as an animated 3D or 2D character rather than as their physical self, typically using real-time motion capture for face and body. The category overlaps with 'VTuber' (virtual YouTuber) and has grown into a distinct entertainment genre with its own audience and conventions.

A subset of motion capture focused specifically on hands and fingers — tracking the position and rotation of each joint to reproduce fine motor movements like pointing, gripping, or in this case, cracking knuckles. It typically requires dedicated hardware such as mocap gloves or high-resolution hand-tracking cameras beyond what full-body systems provide.
